body:
Gujarat as a Centre of Trade

During the medieval and early modern periods, Gujarat was one of the important commercial regions of the Indian subcontinent. Its position on the western coast gave merchants access to the Arabian Sea and the wider Indian Ocean. At the same time, roads connected Gujarat with the markets and production centres of northern and central India and the Deccan.

Gujarat's commercial strength depended on the connection between inland production, markets, transport, banking and overseas shipping. A merchant could obtain cloth from an inland town, transport it to a port, arrange payment through a banker and sell it through commercial contacts in West Asia or elsewhere.

Merchant network

A merchant network is a system of connected traders, producers, markets, transport routes and financial arrangements through which goods and payments move between places.

The Main Commercial Centres

Not every important trading town was a seaport. Different centres performed different functions within Gujarat's economy.

CentreLocation and characterCommercial importance
Cambay (Khambhat)Port on the Gulf of KhambhatMajor earlier outlet for overseas trade
SuratPort on the Tapi River, linked to the Arabian SeaMajor Mughal-period gateway for overseas trade
AhmedabadInland urban centreManufacturing, wholesale trade and connections with northern markets
Bharuch (Broach)Town and port on the Narmada RiverCommercial centre and link in important inland routes

Cambay was prominent before Surat became the leading Mughal-period port. The rise of Surat did not mean that the older trading centres immediately disappeared. Commercial importance changed as political conditions, navigation and transport routes changed.

Why Ports Needed Inland Markets

A port was not necessarily the place where its exported goods were produced. Cotton might be grown in the countryside, processed in one town and woven or dyed in another. Merchants then assembled the finished goods for shipment.

The area supplying goods to a port is called its hinterland. Gujarat's ports served hinterlands extending beyond the present boundaries of Gujarat. Commercial roads linked them to markets in Rajasthan, northern India, Malwa and the northern Deccan.

An emporium was an important commercial centre where goods from different production areas were collected, bought and sold. Surat became such an emporium during the Mughal period.

The Main Period of Development

Cambay was an important port during the Gujarat Sultanate period, especially in the 15th and early 16th centuries. Surat expanded as a major overseas trading centre during the 16th century and became particularly important under the Mughals in the 17th century. European trading companies joined commercial networks that Indian and other Asian merchants had already developed.

Prelims focus

  • Cambay is the historical name of present-day Khambhat.
  • Surat is situated on the Tapi River and traded through the Arabian Sea.
  • Ahmedabad was an important inland commercial centre, not a seaport.
  • Surat became a major western trading emporium during the Mughal period.
  • Trap: Overseas trade depended on inland production and transport; the port itself did not produce every exported commodity.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, Ch. 6, 'Towns, Traders and Craftspersons', pp. 78–84; IGNOU, Early Modern Cities, Unit 29, 'Port Cities: Sixteenth to Eighteenth Centuries', sections 29.2.1–29.2.2, pp. 23–24, consulted 19 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Merchants and transport workers carried goods between Gujarat's inland markets and its ports.

pictures.alt: A network links Gujarat's production centres, Ahmedabad and Bharuch, Cambay and Surat, and overseas markets across the Arabian Sea.

title: Medieval Gujarat's Merchant Networks: How Ports, Markets and Trade Were Connected

body:
Location and Historical Importance

Cambay, known today as Khambhat, is situated on the Gulf of Khambhat. It was an important centre of Gujarat's maritime trade before Surat emerged as the leading Mughal-period port.

In the medieval period, Cambay connected merchants from the Gujarat hinterland with traders operating across the Arabian Sea. It functioned as a market where goods from inland production centres could be assembled for overseas trade.

Cambay's commercial importance was closely connected with the prosperous trading towns of Gujarat and the routes extending towards northern India. Merchants could obtain goods from the interior, bring them to Cambay and arrange their onward movement by sea.

Trade and the Gujarat Hinterland

Cambay handled goods associated with Gujarat's textile-producing and trading economy. The town's importance did not depend solely on local manufacture. Merchants also brought commodities from surrounding regions and more distant markets.

Ahmedabad became an important inland commercial and manufacturing centre during the Gujarat Sultanate period. Its roads connected commercial activity in the interior with the ports of the Gulf of Khambhat.

These relationships explain why a merchant could operate from an inland city while participating in overseas trade. The merchant did not need to own a seagoing ship or live at the port to sell goods in foreign markets.

Navigation and Cambay's Changing Position

The Gulf of Khambhat has strong tidal conditions, and navigation through its waters required care. Larger seagoing vessels could not always operate conveniently at the town's waterfront. Goods could therefore be transferred between larger ships and smaller coastal craft through suitable anchorages.

Historical accounts identify nearby maritime points, including Gogha, among the places associated with the handling of Cambay's trade. The important distinction is between the commercial centre where merchants conducted business and the anchorage where a large ship could safely load or unload.

Silting and navigational difficulties contributed to changes in Cambay's importance. Political and commercial circumstances also mattered. During the 16th century, Surat developed increasingly strong connections with the Mughal-controlled interior and with overseas shipping.

Surat's rise was a gradual shift in commercial importance, not an event that instantly ended trade at Cambay. Both ports belonged to a wider network in which merchants could use different routes and markets.

Cambay and Surat Compared

FeatureCambay (Khambhat)Surat
WaterfrontGulf of KhambhatTapi River and Arabian Sea connections
Period of greatest relative prominenceEarlier medieval and Gujarat Sultanate trade16th–17th-century expansion under the Mughals
Main distinctionOlder maritime commercial centreLeading Mughal-period western trading gateway

Prelims focus

  • Cambay is the former name of Khambhat.
  • Cambay is associated with the Gulf of Khambhat.
  • Cambay was a major maritime commercial centre before Surat's rise.
  • Tidal and silting conditions affected navigation around Cambay.
  • Trap: Cambay and Surat were different ports; neither name refers to Ahmedabad.

[IGNOU, Early Modern Cities, Unit 29, sections 29.2.1–29.2.2, pp. 23–24, consulted 19 November 2026; Gazetteer of the Bombay Presidency, Vol. VI, Cambay, Ch. II, 'Trade and Manufactures', historical trade and harbour sections, 1880, consulted 19 November 2026; NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, Ch. 6, p. 84.]

pictures.alt: Smaller coastal craft link Cambay's trading market with larger ships at suitable anchorages in the strongly tidal Gulf of Khambhat.
pictures.caption: Trade could reach Cambay through smaller vessels even when large ships used other anchorages.

title: Cambay (Khambhat): Gujarat's Earlier Maritime Trading Centre

body:
Why Inland Routes Were Essential

Medieval Gujarat's ports depended on roads reaching agricultural regions, craft-producing towns and major markets. The goods shipped from Surat or Cambay often originated far from the coast. Inland trade also brought imported commodities from the ports to buyers in the interior.

Merchants used roads to transport cloth, grain, dyes and other goods between markets. Pack animals and carts carried commercial loads, while organised groups of travellers helped move goods through territories controlled by different rulers.

Two Important Commercial Connections

Under the Mughals, Surat developed links with markets in northern India and the northern Deccan. Historical descriptions identify two important approaches to Agra:

  • The older western approach: A route involving Bharuch (Broach), Cambay, Ahmedabad and Ajmer connected Gujarat's western commercial centres with Agra.
  • The route through the northern Deccan and central India: Surat was connected with Agra through Burhanpur, Malwa and Gwalior. The Mughal conquest of Khandesh in 1601 helped increase the importance of this connection.

These were major commercial corridors, not the only roads available to merchants. Routes could vary according to the goods being carried, the intended market, political conditions and the security of travel.

Why Burhanpur Mattered

Burhanpur was a significant trading centre in the northern Deccan. Its position helped connect Surat with the interior through Khandesh and Malwa.

When Mughal control extended into Khandesh, Surat's commercial connections with the northern Deccan became easier to organise. The route through Burhanpur provided an important alternative to the older western approach through Cambay and Ahmedabad.

Markets, Transport and Merchant Security

Medieval towns included marketplaces that drew produce from nearby villages. A mandapika, related to the later term mandi, was a market where agricultural and other goods were brought for sale. A hatta, related to haat, referred to a market street or trading area with shops.

Local markets were linked to larger towns. A trader might purchase goods at a small market, transfer them through a wholesale centre and eventually sell them to a merchant supplying an overseas port.

Travel was not always safe. Merchants passed through different kingdoms and sometimes difficult terrain. They therefore often travelled in caravans, groups that could make transport and protection easier to arrange.

The Banjaras were among the trading and transport groups active in the wider Indian subcontinent. Their association with the movement of goods overland should be distinguished from the work of seagoing merchants and shipowners.

Trade Could Move in Both Directions

Inland roads were not simply export routes. Textiles and other products travelled towards Gujarat's ports, while imported goods could move from the coast to consumers in the interior. Banking arrangements also allowed merchants to settle payments across these distant markets.

Prelims focus

  • Surat was connected with Agra through Burhanpur, Malwa and Gwalior.
  • An older route involved Bharuch, Cambay, Ahmedabad and Ajmer.
  • Khandesh came under Mughal control in 1601, strengthening the commercial connection through Burhanpur.
  • Mandapika is associated with a market; hatta with a market street.
  • Caravans helped merchants transport goods and protect their interests.
  • Trap: Burhanpur and Ahmedabad were inland commercial centres, not Arabian Sea ports.

[IGNOU, Early Modern Cities, Unit 29, section 29.2.2, pp. 23–24, consulted 19 November 2026; NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, Ch. 6, 'A Network of Small Towns' and 'Traders Big and Small', pp. 78–80; Gazetteer of the Bombay Presidency, Vol. VI, Cambay, Ch. II, 'Trade and Manufactures', 1880, consulted 19 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Bharuch–Cambay–Ahmedabad–Ajmer and Surat–Burhanpur–Malwa–Gwalior lead to Agra; Mughal control of Khandesh in 1601 strengthened the Burhanpur connection.
pictures.caption: Surat and Cambay were connected with northern markets through different inland corridors.

title: Inland Trade Routes: Connecting Gujarat with Northern India and the Deccan

body:
Surat's Location and Rise

Surat is situated on the Tapi River in Gujarat, with access to the Arabian Sea. Its location allowed it to receive goods from Gujarat's inland markets and from the northern Deccan while maintaining shipping connections across the Indian Ocean.

The Mughals acquired Surat in 1573. During the 16th and 17th centuries, the port developed into a major centre of maritime commerce. The large Mughal hinterland supplied goods for export and created demand for imported products.

Surat became an emporium of western trade: an important centre where merchants bought and sold goods originating in many different places. Its commercial importance extended beyond Gujarat because traders from northern India and overseas markets conducted business there.

Why Surat Was Called the Gate to Mecca

Surat was closely linked with maritime travel to West Asia, including the Hajj pilgrimage. Ships carrying pilgrims departed from Surat towards Red Sea ports such as Jeddah, from which pilgrims continued their journey to Mecca.

For this reason, Surat was described as the gate to Mecca. It was also associated with the title Bandar-i-Mubarak, meaning the blessed port.

The expression gate to Mecca identifies Surat as an important departure point for pilgrims. It does not mean that Mecca was located in Gujarat or directly on the coast.

Surat's Commercial Activities

Surat had retail shops, wholesale markets, warehouses and banking establishments. Indian merchants dealt with overseas buyers, while visiting merchants and the representatives of European trading companies arranged purchases and shipments.

Cotton textiles were among Surat's prominent commercial goods. Cloth with decorative zari, especially gold-lace borders, was particularly well known. Such textiles found markets in West Asia, Africa and Europe.

Surat was also a centre for exchanging goods that were not necessarily produced in the city. Some commodities arrived through inland roads; others came by sea and could be sold onwards through the port's commercial network.

A Cosmopolitan Port City

Surat's population and trading community included people from different religious and regional backgrounds. Hindu and Jain merchants, Muslim trading communities and merchants from overseas all participated in its commerce.

Arab, Persian and European connections added to the city's diversity. In the 17th century, Portuguese, Dutch and English traders maintained factories and warehouses at Surat. These establishments supported trade rather than modern industrial manufacturing.

The movement of merchants, travellers and pilgrims created demand for accommodation, transport, food and other services. Surat therefore combined the functions of a port, commercial market, financial centre and place of pilgrimage departure.

Prelims focus

  • Surat is situated on the Tapi River.
  • The Mughals acquired Surat in 1573.
  • Surat was an important Mughal-period emporium of western trade.
  • Surat was called the gate to Mecca because pilgrim ships departed from the port.
  • Surat textiles were particularly associated with decorative zari borders.
  • Trap: Surat's importance was both commercial and religious; its pilgrim connection was not an alternative to trade.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, Ch. 6, 'A Gateway to the West: Surat', pp. 84–85; IGNOU, Early Modern Cities, Unit 29, sections 29.2.1–29.2.4, pp. 23–25, consulted 19 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Surat attracted Indian and overseas merchants, ships and pilgrims during the Mughal period.
